description:
Two square kundan frames, one above the dial and one below, edged in green enamel and set with cubic zirconia stones at the centre: that's the whole design, repeated top and bottom so the watch reads as symmetrical from either angle. Triple gold chains carry the weight instead of a single strap, and small ghungroo bells sit at the very ends of each chain, close to the wrist rather than dangling loose.

The dial itself is a soft pearlescent white, plain enough not to compete with the framing around it, and still perfectly readable day to day. This is a piece that photographs better than a plain watch ever will, which matters for the kind of festive event where people are actually taking pictures. A saree with gold jewellery already in the mix carries it easily, and it holds its own without needing anything else on that wrist.

The CZ stones are cubic zirconia rather than diamond, and the frames are enamel and kundan-style work over a gold-tone base rather than solid gold, honest terms for a ₹299 piece built around craft rather than raw material cost. The triple-chain construction means it needs a little more care when you put it on and take it off, so the chains don't tangle. Store it flat, away from perfume, and it keeps its shine through the season it was bought for and the next one too.

name: Red Meenakari Tulip Kundan Bracelet Watch
description:
Red is a harder colour to do well in enamel work than green or blue, it can tip into looking flat instead of rich, and this one avoids that: bold red meenakari tulip motifs, teardrop kundan-style stones at their centres, framing a plain white quartz dial that stays out of the way. Triple gold chains hold it together, with cascading ghungroo bells at both ends rather than just one.

The tulip shape is doing real work here. It's a softer, more floral motif than the square or diamond-panel designs elsewhere in this kind of watch, and it reads warmer on the wrist because of it, less geometric, more like something painted by hand, which is closer to what it actually is. Wear it with festive red or gold, where the tulips pick up the same family of colour rather than fighting it, at a wedding or a Diwali evening where a plain watch would look underdressed.

The kundan is kundan-style stonework rather than the traditional uncut-diamond technique, set in enamel over a gold-tone chain rather than solid gold, and that honesty is what keeps a ₹369 price believable for this much detail. The chains cascade rather than sit flat, so give them a moment to settle when you put it on, and keep the panels away from water and perfume so the enamel colour holds. It's built for the handful of occasions a year that actually call for this much jewellery on one wrist.

name: Red Kundan Charm Bracelet Watch, Floral Pendant
description:
Not every piece here uses a painted panel to frame the dial; this one uses charms instead, small red tulip kundan-style shapes sitting just above and below a plain white quartz face, with a separate grey floral kundan pendant hanging lower on a double gold chain. It's a busier silhouette than a single-panel watch, more like a charm bracelet that happens to tell the time.

That looseness is the appeal. The pendant swings slightly rather than sitting fixed in place, and the double chain (thinner than the triple-chain designs) keeps the whole thing lighter on the wrist despite having more individual pieces attached to it. Ghungroo bells finish it off, giving a soft sound with movement rather than a loud jingle. It suits an outfit that already has some red or gold running through it, a festive kurta set or wedding-season saree, where the charm and pendant read as one coordinated idea rather than two.

The kundan on both the charms and the pendant is kundan-style stonework over a gold-tone base, and the grey in the pendant is enamel colour rather than a separate metal, honest terms for a ₹399 piece built on detail rather than raw materials. Because there's more moving hardware here than a single-panel watch, check the charms sit straight after putting it on, and keep it away from water and perfume so the enamel keeps its colour through the season.

Yellow reads differently to red or blue meenakari; it photographs brighter and suits a daytime festival look better than an evening one. Wear it to a Diwali morning gathering or a mehendi function where the outfit already leans towards yellow, orange or green, and let the elephant do the work of a conversation starter, it's a small enough charm to notice up close rather than shout from across a room. The pearl border around the dial is a nice detail that a lot of these watches skip.

The green in both the leaf accents and the elephant is meenakari enamel colour rather than a separate stone, and the whole piece sits on a gold-tone base rather than solid gold, honest terms for a ₹399 piece that's really about the folk-art detailing. Keep the enamel away from water and perfume, and give the cascading chains a second to settle when you first put it on so nothing tangles.

description:

Polki kundan centres and separate kundan-style medallion beads add two more layers of stonework, and cascading chains end in ghungroo bells.

Of everything in this range, this is the one built to be seen from across a room rather than admired up close, the stone-set dial edge alone catches more light than a plain frame does. It wants an equally bold outfit, blue or gold festive wear rather than anything muted, and it suits an evening function more than a daytime one simply because that's when the sparkle actually reads. If you're only buying one statement bracelet watch this wedding season, the density of detail here makes the case for this one.

Polki kundan is a style term for this look rather than a claim about the stones themselves, and the CZ stones are cubic zirconia, not diamond, set over a gold-tone chain base. At ₹399, the honest sell is craft density rather than material value, and there's genuinely a lot packed onto one wrist. With this much stonework, keep it away from water, perfume, and rough handling, and store it separately so the medallion beads don't catch on other jewellery.

name: Blush Pink Glass Jelly Bangles, Set of Eight
description:
Jelly bangles get their name from the finish, not the material, a glossy, faintly translucent glass that catches light the way a hard resin never quite does. This set of eight comes in a soft blush pink, stacked close enough that they move as one block on the wrist rather than eight separate rings knocking against each other.

Glass bangles are a genuinely different wearing experience to metal ones. They're cooler against the skin in warm weather, and the sound they make sliding together is softer and higher-pitched than a metal stack, closer to what you'd hear at a wedding function where a whole row of women are wearing exactly this kind of set. Available in sizes 2.4, 2.6 and 2.8, so measure an existing bangle before ordering rather than guessing; glass doesn't stretch the way an adjustable metal band would.

Being glass, it's the one honest trade-off worth saying plainly: these are more fragile than an alloy bangle stack, so slide them on gently over the knuckle rather than forcing a tight fit, and expect to treat them the way you'd treat any glass bangle set passed down at a wedding, worn and put away carefully rather than knocked around daily. At ₹220 for eight, that's still a full stack of colour for less than a single metal cuff costs, which is really the appeal of jelly bangles as a category.

Keep it away from moisture and perfume, and store it somewhere dry so the plating holds its finish. For the price, it's a reasonable way to add one geometric, slightly-more-dressed-up piece to a jewellery rotation that's mostly simpler daily pieces.

name: Gold-Toned Crystal Tennis Bracelet & Snake Chain Combo

specs.stone: Glass or cubic zirconia, unclear from text

specs.care instructions: Keep dry; store safely in a dry place after every wear

description:
One of these two bracelets is built for shine, cubic zirconia stones set edge to edge along a gold-toned band so the stones do the talking. The other skips stones altogether, a flat, close-linked snake chain in the same gold-toned finish, smooth enough to catch light on its own without any help. Together they read like two different moods rather than a matched pair, one bracelet for when you want sparkle at the wrist and one for the days you'd rather keep things quiet. That's the whole idea.

Both pieces are gold-toned metal over a base that isn't specified further, so treat them as everyday stacking pieces rather than a lifetime one. The tennis-style strand sits close and doesn't move around much once it's on, while the snake chain has more drape to it, the kind that settles flat against the skin instead of standing up. Layer them on one wrist for a fuller look, or split the pair, sparkle on one arm and the plain chain on the other, and let each do its own job.

At this price a set like this earns its keep by giving two genuinely different bracelets rather than two versions of the same idea. Wear the tennis strand to a family function where a bit of shine is expected, and save the snake chain for the office or a plain kurta day when you'd rather not announce it.

Keep both pieces dry and store them away from perfume and moisture after wear, the usual rule for gold-toned plating at any price. Small habits like that stretch the life of a set like this more than anything printed on the card.

name: Gold-Toned Halo Nath with Clear Stones

specs.stone: Glass or cubic zirconia, unclear from text
specs.care instructions: Keep away from moisture and perfumes; store safely in a dry place after every wear

description:
A ring of stones set edge to edge all the way round is what turns a plain hoop into a halo, and that's the whole design here, no separate motif worked into the metal, just density. The gold-toned wire underneath barely shows through the clear stones, so from a few feet away the piece reads as one continuous circle of sparkle rather than a hoop with stones added on. A single teardrop stone hangs just below the ring, catching light on its own once the halo settles.

This is built for occasions where a plain stud would get lost. A dense ring of stones photographs well even in low light, the kind a lot of festive and wedding functions are lit with, and it holds its own next to heavier jewellery elsewhere on the face without competing for attention. On a quieter day it's a lot for a plain kurta, so save it for when the rest of the outfit can carry the weight.

The stones are cubic zirconia rather than diamond, set into a plain plated base with no special coating claimed beyond that, so treat it the way you'd treat any plated piece. Wipe it after wear and keep it clear of perfume before it goes on, a small habit that's cheap insurance either way. It's a piece built to be the loudest thing on the face, and at this price that's not much of an ask.

It suits the same kind of occasion a gold halo nath would, a wedding, a big festive day, anywhere the rest of the face is already carrying jewellery and needs one piece dense enough to hold its own rather than get lost in the mix. Pair it with a heavier silver-toned set elsewhere, earrings or a maang tikka, so the metal tones agree with each other instead of competing. It sits well against a silver-heavy lehenga or a plain white-and-silver saree, where a gold-toned piece would have stood out for the wrong reason.

The stones are cubic zirconia, not the real thing, set into a plated base with no special coating claimed beyond the plating itself. Wipe it down after wear and keep it away from perfume, the way you would with any plated piece. It's a small, deliberate cost for a piece doing this much work at this price.

This one builds a small floral cluster into the metal itself, a grouping of round and marquise-cut clear stones shaped like a flower, sitting just off to one side of the hoop rather than running evenly around it. A single teardrop-cut stone hangs below the cluster on a short drop, echoing the marquise shapes rather than repeating the round ones.

The floral shape carries more visual weight on one side of the ring than a plain halo design does, which suits a bigger occasion, a wedding day or a festive function, where the face is already dressed up and can carry a denser detail near the nose. It photographs with more definition than an evenly set ring too, since the cluster catches light from more angles at once.

Keep it dry, keep it away from perfume, and store it somewhere it won't get knocked around by heavier jewellery; the marquise stones sit slightly proud of the setting and are the first place a scratch would show. At ₹109, the floral cluster is doing more design work than the price implies, and it's the kind of piece worth keeping for the occasions that actually call for it rather than wearing daily.

That makes it easy to wear with something already detailed, a printed kurta or a patterned saree, without the jewellery competing for attention.

Enamel wants gentler handling than a plated stone-set piece; avoid contact with perfume, keep it away from direct water, and store it somewhere it won't rub against harder jewellery, since a chip in enamel doesn't come back the way a scratch on plating sometimes fades. At ₹285 for three pieces working as a set, that's roughly what a single well-made pendant costs elsewhere.

Gold-toned vine work climbs across the surface, small flowers with dark centres worked into the metal rather than sitting as separate stones.

It's a rigid, hinged bangle rather than a flexible bracelet, the kind that opens on one side and closes shut around the wrist instead of sliding on. The enamel sits over an anti-tarnish base, so the colour is built to hold rather than fade the way cheaper painted finishes tend to after a few months of wear.

name: Pink Tulip Pendant Necklace

specs.stone: Glass or cubic zirconia, unclear from text

description:
A tulip is a literal shape to build a pendant around, and this one commits to it: a single pink stone forms the closed bud, cut to a point at the top the way a tulip petal folds, with two small clear stones angled below as leaves on a curved gold-toned stem. Nothing about the shape is abstracted into a vaguer flower motif; it reads as a tulip immediately.

The stones are cubic zirconia or glass rather than anything gem-grade, set into a gold-finished snake chain, the tightly coiled link style that lies flatter against the skin than an open cable chain does. That flatness matters more on a longer pendant like this one, where the chain does more visible work than a short choker chain would.

Tulips carry a slightly different weight than roses do in jewellery, less bound to romance specifically and more to spring and renewal generally, which makes this a fair pick for a birthday or a small gift rather than only a romantic one. It sits well against a plain neckline, kurta or western wear equally, since the pink is soft enough not to fight with most other colours nearby it.

Keep it dry and away from perfume, and give the chain occasional care since a snake chain can kink if it's balled up rather than laid flat in storage. At ₹210, the literal tulip shape is doing more design work than an abstract flower pendant at the same price usually manages.

description:
Most lockets in this catalogue hang from a chain; this one sits on a ring instead, a heart-shaped, openable locket built into an adjustable band rather than a pendant. The band is gold-finished copper, open at the back so it isn't sized to a specific finger, and adjusts to fit most hands the way an open ring does.

What opens is genuinely functional rather than decorative: the source material confirms the locket takes replaceable inserts, a different mechanism from the name-engraving personalisation some lockets offer. This one is built to swap what sits inside rather than have anything written on it. The heart itself has a faceted, glass-like clear front over whatever's placed inside, catching light the way a cut surface does rather than sitting flat.

A ring built around a locket rather than a stone is an unusual enough shape that it works better as a considered gift than an everyday basic; the open-back sizing also makes it easy to give without knowing an exact ring size in advance, which most rings don't allow for. It suits someone who already has enough plain rings and wants one that does something different.

Keep it away from water where possible, since an openable mechanism has more places for moisture to sit than a solid band does, and check the fit stays snug rather than loose after the first few wears. At ₹499, this is one of the pricier pieces in the range, and the working locket mechanism is the reason why.

An upside-down rose carries a specific, slightly wistful reading in flower symbolism, generally taken as remembrance rather than a fresh bloom, which makes this a fair pick for jewellery bought to mark something rather than to simply decorate an outfit. name: Pearl-Look Tulip Toggle Clasp Bracelet
description:
The clasp is the whole design here, not an afterthought bolted onto a plain string of beads. It's a toggle in the T-and-ring style jewellers call OT, shaped and enamelled into a small pink and green tulip, sitting at the front of the wrist rather than hidden at the back the way most clasps are. Everything else is a single strand of faux pearl beads, baroque rather than perfectly round. It reads as pearl at a glance, each bead catching light a little differently as the wrist moves.

Baroque is the honest word for beads with a slightly irregular, dimpled surface rather than a true sphere. It's part of what makes imitation pearl read as pearl-like instead of plastic, and it's the same rough shape real freshwater pearls take before anyone sorts them for uniformity. These are faux, not the sea- or farm-grown kind, threaded on a fine strand with the tulip toggle doing the closing.

A toggle clasp needs a slightly looser fit than one that locks flush, since the bar has to pass through the ring to fasten, worth knowing before you order a size. It suits the kind of outfit that wants one quiet, considered piece rather than several competing ones: a plain kurta sleeve, a saree blouse cuff, a daytime function rather than a full evening one.

Keep it away from water and perfume, the way any plated or coated finish prefers, and store it flat rather than balled up so the strand doesn't kink near the clasp. At ₹199, the tulip toggle is doing real design work that a plain bar-and-ring closure wouldn't.

Cat's eye is a real optical effect, a band of light that moves across a stone as it turns, and in fine jewellery it usually comes from genuine chrysoberyl. This bracelet borrows the name for a fiber-optic glass bead instead, cut to give a similar milky sheen and a moving line of light without the mineral behind it. It sits at the centre of a small vine of gold-plated copper, tiny pave leaves branching off on either side, with a couple of clear stones set close by.

The base metal is gold-plated copper, and the closure is a pull-chain style rather than a clasp: you slide the bead along the chain to tighten or loosen the fit, which makes it genuinely one-size, no clasp to fumble with one-handed. That's worth knowing before you order, since it behaves differently on the wrist than a fixed-length bracelet does.

The glass bead itself has real presence despite being small, a soft, cloudy glow rather than the hard sparkle of a faceted stone, which makes it sit quietly against skin rather than demanding attention. It reads well on its own, worn daily, or stacked with a plainer band on the same wrist.

Keep it away from water and perfume, the way plated pieces need, and slide the pull-chain closed rather than tugging at the vine itself to adjust the fit. At ₹220, the honest note is that the cat's eye effect here is glass doing a very good impression of a stone most people will never actually own.

name: Pink Enamel Tulip Charm Bracelet
description:
A single enamelled tulip hangs at the centre of a fine gold-toned snake chain here, bright pink petals with two green leaves below, painted rather than set with a stone. Enamel gives the colour a glassy, slightly domed finish, closer to how a real tulip petal catches light than a flat-painted charm would, and it's the whole design rather than one detail among several.

The chain is a snake-link style, tightly coiled metal that lies flat against the wrist instead of standing proud the way an open cable chain can. It's a plain setting for the charm on purpose, nothing else competing with the single tulip for attention.

Bright pink reads cheerful rather than formal, which suits this piece for daytime wear more than an evening one: office hours with a cotton kurta, a college day, a weekend where the outfit is simple and the bracelet does the one job of adding colour. It's a small piece, so it layers easily with a plainer band or watch on the same wrist without crowding either.

Enamel isn't indestructible glass, so avoid knocking it against hard surfaces, and keep it away from perfume and water, which can dull any plated finish over time. Wipe it after wear rather than leaving it to sit against damp skin.

At ₹199, a single well-made charm does more for a bracelet than several smaller motifs would at the same price, and the pink here is confident enough to not need company.

The petals and two leaves are enamelled onto a gold-plated frame, glassy rather than matte, catching a small highlight where the light hits the curve of each petal.

Unlike a snake-chain bracelet, this one closes with a lobster clasp, the small spring-loaded hook most people already know how to work one-handed. It's a plainer, more secure closure than a toggle, useful if you'd rather not think about the clasp again once it's on.

The gold-plated finish sits under the enamel rather than a stone setting, so the whole piece is one continuous surface with nothing to catch or loosen over time the way a prong-set stone can. The single tulip stays the whole point of the design; nothing else on the chain competes with it for attention.

Rose reads well against gold jewellery generally and doesn't fight with most Indian wear colours nearby it, from a plain cream kurta to a deeper festive saree. It suits gifting as easily as it suits buying for yourself, since the colour reads considered rather than loud.

Keep it away from perfume and water, which dull enamel and plating over time, and wipe it dry after wear. At ₹199, this sits as the slightly more grown-up sibling to a brighter pink tulip charm in the same range, same idea, different mood.

description:

The tulip is enamel, painted onto a gold-finished frame rather than built from a stone, which gives it a glassy, slightly domed surface instead of the flat sheen a printed charm would have. Two small green leaves sit below the bud on a short stem, keeping the whole pendant compact rather than a large statement drop.

The chain is a snake-link style, coiled metal that sits flat against the collarbone. That flatness matters on a pendant that hangs at chest height, since a bulkier chain would compete visually with a small charm like this one instead of just carrying it.

Blush pink is quiet by design. It sits well under a plain neckline, a saree blouse, or a simple western top, and it doesn't demand a matching outfit the way a bolder colour might. It reads as everyday jewellery rather than occasion-only, something you'd wear on a normal Tuesday as easily as to a small family function.

Keep it away from water and perfume, and store it flat so the chain doesn't tangle. At ₹210, it's the gentlest option in a small family of tulip pieces that range from pastel to deep red.
